text.p: Following are the main stories in Slovenia's Friday morning newspapers:
- European Cultural Month, during which over 250 cultural events will take place in Slovenia's capital, started in Ljubljana on Thursday.

- The Social Democrats, the largest opposition party, said they would not participate in parliamentary sessions until at least Tuesday in protest over the body's decision not to elect a member of the party as head of the parliamentary commitee for budget control.

- The government said at least 70 percent of all trains must run during a ten-day railway strike which is expected to start on May 20. Railway employees demand higher salaries but the government insists it cannot meet their demands.
- The key benefit of joining the European Union is the peace and stability that membership brings, Swedish Foreign Minister Lena Hjelm-Wallen said during a visit to Slovenia.
- March gross monthly salaries rose 1.3 percent compared to February and 15.3 percent compared to March last year, the Statistical Office said.
- Slovenia's wood processor Inles said it would be forced to file for bankruptcy if the state did not help it improve liquidity. The company said it needed a loan of $0.6 million.

- Experts said it was unlikely that most Slovenian estates would be registered in the national real estate register by a legal deadline of July 2,000 on the basis of a poor track record in registering new buildings in the past.
- President Milan Kucan on Thursday attended a celebration marking the sixth anniversary of the establishment of army training centers in Slovenia.
- The government on Thursday refused to increase prices of natural gas. Gas firms demanded an increase of nine percent.
- Economists said a failure by Slovenia to ratify the association agreement with the European Union in the next couple of weeks would slow the country's economic growth.
